extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (authors of papers, books, lectures; researchers and advanced students)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing mathematics (papers, books, lectures): how to plan, draft, organize, notate, and revise mathematical exposition so it communicates ideas clearly to a chosen audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Say something
rubrics_metrics.description: You must have something to say — the basic ingredient of good exposition is that the work actually conveys a coherent subject or central idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the two 'diseases': (a) saying nothing (pages of words that convey no idea), and (b) trying to say too many unrelated things (overly broad works that lack a unifying subject). Organize around a single central idea, and ensure the material 'hangs together' so the reader can grasp what the work is about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for a specific audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide who you are writing for and tailor motivation, formality, repetition, and explanations accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify the audience as precisely as practical (a friendly colleague, topologists, second-year grad students, a particular person). An intended reader determines how much motivation, informality, or repetition is necessary. Anticipate the reader's difficulties and avoid writing that is either too inclusive and vague or so narrow as to be needlessly polemical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize first (plan and outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before detailed composition, organize the subject: decide main headings, subheadings, what goes under each, and how parts connect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make an outline in which theorems, lemmas, remarks, proofs, corollaries, examples have places; aim for logical correctness and psychological digestibility. Organize around central examples and counterexamples; avoid throwing in too much detail too early. Organization is more important than linear arrangement, and a good outline makes reading and teaching easy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think about the alphabet (design notation carefully)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose notation deliberately and consistently up front; good, consistent notation greatly aids exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate symbols for points, sets, functions, indices, surfaces, etc. Avoid ad hoc mid-sentence notation changes, 'frozen' or overloaded letters, and alphabetic dissonance (e.g., near collisions of glyph meanings). Maintain an 'alphabetical harmony' so the reader is not distracted by confusing symbol choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in spirals (draft, then rewrite repeatedly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose by the spiral plan: write chapters/sections in order, then revisit earlier parts repeatedly — rewrite whole sections rather than patch-editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First drafts: spill your heart, write fast, violate rules. Later drafts: rewrite completely (every word, large omissions if necessary). Expect multiple rewrites (some chapters many times). Use the first drafts to discover structure and the rewrites to organize and polish. Rewriting means write again, not merely mark edits with a pencil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize always (continuously refine organization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organization is ongoing: keep refining the outline, arrangement, and logical order as you write and discover new connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subplots, motifs, and gradual introductions (mention a concept earlier, expand later) to prepare the reader. Ensure logical dependencies are ordered so no sheet or statement appears before what it requires; rearrange as the work grows to maintain efficient, pleasant flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use central concrete examples and counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Base exposition on key concrete examples and instructive counterexamples rather than excessive abstraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Big general thoughts should be motivated by small, profound examples. Organize around central examples; point out where proofs do not apply and where counterexamples guide future directions. Avoid filling exposition with minutiae that help only the already-knowledgeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write good language (correct grammar, diction, punctuation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use correct, commonly accepted language style—grammar, word choice, and punctuation matter and should not distract the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell correctly, follow standard usage (subtle differences like 'that' vs 'which', 'less' vs 'fewer'), and avoid pedantic, flowery, or bureaucratic prose. Learn and live with the vernacular of your audience's language (English, French, etc.). Small consistent errors accumulate and harm clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty about status of statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Always tell the reader the status of claims: what is proved, what is asserted without proof, what will be proved later, and what is yet unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't gloss over difficulties or bluff. If a proof is cumbersome, warn the reader (e.g. 'unfortunately the only known proof is the following cumbersome computation'). If you claim something is 'obvious', be sure it really is — or explain why. Provide references when appropriate and keep the reader in your confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irrelevant assumptions and trivial clutter
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not introduce irrelevant hypotheses, extraneous assumptions, or needless complications that distract readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State and exclude trivial cases explicitly if necessary; avoid gratuitous conditions that confuse emphasis. Irrelevant labels, assumptions, or reminders can mislead and waste the reader's time. Emphasize what matters and minimize the trivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be parsimonious with labels and displays
rubrics_metrics.description: Use labels (equation numbers, displayed formulas) sparingly and meaningfully so labels serve future reference rather than draw unnecessary attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlabelling attracts the reader's curiosity about why a label is there; underlabelling or misplaced labels is also confusing. Be stingy but consistent: label displays that are referred to later, and avoid pointless numbered displays that distract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make proofs human-understandable (forward exposition, explain heuristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write proofs so a human reader can follow the reasoning: give the idea and the forward argument, not a reverse-verification chain of equalities only checkable by a machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid backward proofs that start from the result and work backwards in a way that is opaque to a reader. Use explanatory paragraphs that outline the method ('first substitute..., then collect terms,...'), present typical small cases to show the pattern (e.g., prove 3x3 then generalize), and avoid long chains of symbolic manipulations without commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symbols and punctuation correctly and consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign consistent meanings to symbols and punctuate symbolic sentences as you would verbal sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide a single verbal reading for each symbol (e.g., read 'in' for ∈), use punctuation with symbolic expressions (commas, periods) consistent with logical structure, avoid starting sentences awkwardly with lone symbols (prefer 'Assume that...'), and use 'then' with 'if' where it aids clarity. Small punctuation choices can prevent backtracking and confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance prose and mathematical displays
rubrics_metrics.description: Interleave prose and displayed mathematics so the eye and brain can process ideas; avoid pages drowning in symbols or excessive prose-only descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use displays to give the eye a chance to help the brain; use prose to explain the significance of displays; avoid overusing suffixes and notation that make the page look like computational hash. The golden mean: enough displays to aid comprehension but enough prose to explain them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt exposition to the medium (lecture vs paper)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize differences between written and oral exposition and adapt content and omission accordingly while keeping the same core goals of content, aim, and organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lectures need omission, pacing, and live feedback; readers can wander and later pick up threads; lectures demand continuous attention. The essential ingredients (content, aim, organization, grammar, notation) remain the same but their application differs with medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defend your style choices against editors/copyreaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to defend deliberate stylistic or notational choices during copyediting so that mathematical meaning is not corrupted by mechanical editing rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial assistants may 'mechanically' apply typographical or grammatical rules that change mathematical meaning (e.g., misapplied hyphens, wrong rewrites). Go forearmed into copyediting and insist on preserving correct mathematical sense; choose and explain your preferred conventions where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when to stop (proofread, let manuscript ripen, then stop)
rubrics_metrics.description: After careful proofreading, verification of computations, and a period of letting the manuscript 'ripen', stop revising and prepare for publication; avoid endless polishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put the manuscript out of sight for some months, then re-read from a rested point of view; check language and mathematics, proofread, and fix obvious major defects. Do not chase mirages of 'one more improvement' — be ruthless in finishing the work and submitting it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use section titles and daily planning to sustain steady writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Prime the pump for steady writing by preparing short section titles and planning the next session's content to maintain momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End each session with a concrete plan (title or first sentence) for the next section; this helps daily continuity and overcomes inertia. Even small daily output steadily accumulates into substantial work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reader's aids after major rewrites
rubrics_metrics.description: After substantial rewrites, prepare mechanical but indispensable reader's aids (table of contents, index, list of prerequisites) to make the final manuscript usable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once you have a stable third (or later) version, add indices, TOC, and other aids; these help readers and typists producing the final typescript. Minor layout rewrites after this stage should be minimal.
